claims.text: Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles contain short-range compositional fluctuations at surfaces and grain boundaries.
These compositional fluctuations cause different local configurations to partially melt at distinct temperatures.
Sequential local melting produces a multi-step premelting transition and broadens the overall melting range relative to unary or binary nanoparticles.
The initial material consists of 5–20 nm Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles with a nominal single-phase solid solution at ambient conditions.
In situ TEM coupled with DSC can track structural and calorimetric changes through premelting and melting.
Heating from room temperature to approximately 1400 °C under inert conditions will cover the anticipated melting regime while minimizing oxidation.
Local compositional gradients near surfaces and interfaces generate multiple partial-melting hot spots.
A multiple-principal-element architecture increases elemental diffusion at surfaces and interfaces.
Enhanced diffusion at surfaces and interfaces triggers partial melting at successively lower temperatures and creates a broad premelting regime.
Chemical complexity can alter alloy liquid configurations and miscibility.
Relative to size-matched Ni or Fe–Ni nanoparticles, Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will show multiple discrete DSC endotherms and stepwise partial melting in TEM.
The Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will exhibit at least two distinct partial-melt ranges before becoming fully molten.
Size-matched unary Ni or binary Fe–Ni nanoparticles will show a single, narrower melting transition with few or no partial-melting steps.
The proposed behavior should occur primarily at similar nanoparticle sizes, moderate heating rates, and inert or vacuum conditions where oxidation does not dominate.
Increasing particle size or drastically changing composition may weaken or eliminate the proposed behavior.
Five-element mixtures can form single-phase nanoparticles more readily than binary mixtures under limited-mobility synthesis conditions.
The temperatures of the partial-melting steps may depend on synthesis, particle-size dispersion, and interfacial chemistry.
Absence of compositional gradients and multi-step transitions, together with identical single sharp melting events in the high-entropy and baseline particles, would invalidate the hypothesis.
